Section 1: Auto Scaling Concept & Architecture

Auto Scaling (Elastic Scaling Service - ESS)

Auto Scaling (Elastic Scaling Service - ESS) is a fully managed cloud service that automatically adjusts compute capacity to match fluctuating business demands and policies.

Compared to traditional static infrastructure requiring expensive over-provisioning for peak traffic, Auto Scaling dynamically creates, configures, and terminates ECS instances or serverless ECI containers in real time. It seamlessly synchronizes with Server Load Balancers (SLB/ALB) and ApsaraDB RDS whitelists, eliminating manual operational bottlenecks while maximizing cost efficiency.

⚡ Elastic Scale-Out

Instantly provisions additional compute resources during traffic surges to maintain consistent application SLAs.

📉 Elastic Scale-In

Automatically releases or stops idle instances during off-peak periods, preventing cloud budget waste.

🛡️ Elastic Self-Healing

Continuously inspects instance health and automatically replaces failed or unhealthy instances without human intervention.

🧠 Intelligent Triggers

Combines CloudMonitor metrics, scheduled timers, target tracking, and AI-driven predictive scaling algorithms.

🔄 Zero-Touch Ecosystem

Automatically registers instances with SLB/ALB backend groups and manages private IP whitelists on RDS databases.

Section 1: Auto Scaling Concept & Architecture

The Elastic Scaling Imperative

The Fixed Capacity Dilemma

Traditional enterprise datacenters rely on fixed static hardware sizing, resulting in two fundamental operational failures:

  • Severe Idle Waste (Trough Hours): Sizing infrastructure for peak loads (e.g. 100 servers) means 70-80% of capacity sits idle during night and weekend troughs, burning unnecessary budget.
  • Catastrophic Outages (Traffic Surges): Unpredicted demand spikes (flash sales, viral marketing, DDoS) overwhelm static compute capacity, causing high latency, packet drops, and complete system crashes.
  • Slow Manual Provisioning: Manually acquiring, racking, imaging, and configuring servers takes days to weeks—far too slow for modern digital business.

The Auto Scaling Solution: Dynamic Curve Alignment

Auto Scaling dynamically mirrors your actual real-time business demand curve:

  • Right-Sized Capacity: Compute resources automatically expand when traffic grows and contract when traffic subsides.
  • High Availability Assurance: Ensures that application performance and response latency remain within contractual SLA thresholds.
  • Massive Cost Reduction: Eliminates continuous over-provisioning costs; organizations only pay for compute units actually utilized during demand windows.
  • Operational Freedom: Automates full lifecycle provisioning, health recovery, load balancer attachment, and network isolation.
Architectural Principle Elasticity is the defining characteristic of cloud computing. Auto Scaling transforms compute capacity from a fixed capital expense (CapEx) into a fluid, automated operational capability (OpEx) that scales with business growth.
Section 1: Auto Scaling Concept & Architecture

Core Scaling Modes

1. Elastic Scale-Out

Automatically expands compute capacity during peak load:

  • Triggered By: CloudMonitor alarms (e.g. CPU > 80%), scheduled timers, or target tracking policies.
  • Actions: Provisions new ECS instances or serverless ECI pods based on the active Scaling Configuration.
  • Integration: Automatically adds new instances to SLB backend server groups and injects private IPs into RDS security whitelists.

2. Elastic Scale-In

Automatically reduces compute capacity during off-peak periods:

  • Triggered By: Low utilization metrics (e.g. CPU < 25%) or scheduled cron expiration.
  • Actions: Safely drains traffic, removes instances from SLB/RDS, and either terminates (Release Mode) or stops them (Shutdown Mode).
  • Cost Impact: Immediately stops hourly/per-second billing on surplus instances.

3. Elastic Self-Healing

Autonomous unhealthy instance replacement:

  • Detection: Regularly inspects ECS running state and SLB health check results across the cluster.
  • Remediation: When an instance fails (hardware fault, OS lockup, or SLB unhealthy status), Auto Scaling automatically removes and replaces it.
  • Zero Human Intervention: Restores healthy cluster capacity without waking up on-call engineers.
Autonomous Health Verification Auto Scaling checks instance status every few minutes. If an instance enters a non-Running state or fails SLB health checks, it is flagged as unhealthy and replaced according to group policy.
Section 1: Auto Scaling Concept & Architecture

The Auto Scaling Triad

1. Scaling Group

The container and boundary manager:

  • Defines capacity limits: MinSize, MaxSize, and Desired Capacity.
  • Binds to specific VPC VSwitches across multi-AZ fault domains.
  • Maintains associated SLB load balancers and RDS database instances.
  • Defines default cooldown time and instance removal policies.

2. Scaling Configuration

The resource blueprint & specification:

  • Specifies ECS instance types (or multi-type lists), CPU/RAM ratios, and generation.
  • Defines system image (Custom Image or Public OS) and storage disk tiers (ESSD).
  • Assigns Security Groups, SSH Key Pairs, RAM Roles, and Cloud-init User Data.
  • A Scaling Group can store up to 10 configurations, with 1 active configuration.

3. Scaling Rules

The operational action triggers:

  • Defines specific scaling steps: e.g., Add 2 instances, Remove 1 instance, or Adjust to 10 instances.
  • Supports Simple Rules, Target Tracking Rules, Step Scaling, and Predictive Rules.
  • Executed via Scheduled Tasks, CloudMonitor Alarm Tasks, or direct OpenAPI calls.
Section 1: Auto Scaling Concept & Architecture

Scaling Activity Lifecycle & Atomicity

Activity Execution Principles

Whenever a scaling rule or trigger fires, a Scaling Activity is generated to add or remove instances:

  • Single Activity Concurrency: A Scaling Group can execute only ONE scaling activity at a time. Concurrent trigger requests are rejected or queued.
  • Non-Interruptible Execution: Once a scaling activity starts, it cannot be aborted mid-flight. If a rule to add 10 instances is executing, it must complete before any other activity can run.
  • Boundary Clamping: Scaling activities strictly respect group limits. If a rule requests Add 5, but current capacity is 8 and MaxSize=10, Auto Scaling automatically adjusts the activity to create only 2 instances.

Rollback & Instance Integrity Rule

How Auto Scaling handles partial provisioning failures during scale-out:

  • Instance Integrity Over Activity Integrity: If an activity attempts to add 10 instances, but 1 instance fails to join the SLB backend, the system rolls back the failed instance only, not the entire activity. The 9 successfully attached instances remain active in service.
  • Cost Responsibility: Because Auto Scaling provisions ECS instances via standard RAM APIs on your behalf, any provisioned instance that ran before rollback will incur standard usage billing for its active minutes.
  • Inventory Retry: If multi-instance types are configured, Auto Scaling automatically attempts fallback types before failing the activity.
Strict Architectural Constraint Because only one scaling activity can execute at any time, avoid configuring overlapping scheduled tasks with identical start times. Set distinct launch expiration windows so tasks can wait for active scaling activities to release the group lock.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Scaling Group Anatomy & Boundaries

Core Capacity Parameters

Parameter Architectural Role Behavior & Constraints
MinSize Minimum Instance Floor The minimum number of instances always maintained in the group. If total instances drop below MinSize, Auto Scaling immediately creates instances to reach it.
MaxSize Maximum Instance Ceiling The absolute upper capacity limit. Scaling activities will clamp and never exceed this ceiling, preventing runaway cloud costs.
Desired Capacity Expected Operating Level Maintains a specific target number of healthy instances between MinSize and MaxSize without requiring rule triggers.
Total Capacity Live Running Count The current sum of auto-created and manually attached instances currently in the group.

Initialization & Dynamic Capacity Rules

Key operational behaviors when configuring scaling group capacity:

  • Auto-Creation on Enable: If an active scaling group has MinSize = 2, but current total capacity is 0, Auto Scaling immediately triggers an activity upon enabling to provision 2 Pay-As-You-Go instances.
  • Equal Min & Max (Fixed Size): Setting MinSize = MaxSize = N creates a fixed-size cluster with self-healing. If any instance fails, Auto Scaling automatically replaces it to keep capacity exactly at N.
  • Dynamic Adjustment: Modifying MinSize or MaxSize on an active group instantly triggers scaling activities to align the current capacity with the new boundary constraints.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Scaling Group Lifecycle States

1. Active State

The scaling group is fully operational and healthy:

  • Monitors capacity and responds to CloudMonitor alarms, scheduled tasks, and scaling rules.
  • Executes scaling activities to maintain capacity within [MinSize, MaxSize].
  • Performs periodic health checks and replaces unhealthy instances.
  • Can only be activated when an active Scaling Configuration or Launch Template is assigned.

2. Inactive State

The scaling group is temporarily paused/disabled:

  • All scaling rules, alarm triggers, and scheduled tasks are rejected.
  • No new scaling activities will be executed.
  • Existing ECS instances remain running in their current state (billing continues).
  • Can only be disabled when no scaling activity is actively executing.

3. Deleting State

The group is undergoing teardown and deletion:

  • Cascading Deletion: Deleting a scaling group permanently deletes its Scaling Configurations, Scaling Rules, and Scaling Activities.
  • Preserved Assets: Deleting a scaling group DOES NOT delete associated SLB load balancers, RDS databases, or CloudMonitor alarm rules.
  • ForceDelete Mode: Auto-releases all auto-created instances while detaching manual instances.
Maintenance Best Practice Disable the scaling group (Inactive State) before executing planned database schema migrations or core application upgrades. This prevents Auto Scaling from spinning up outdated instances while deployment is in progress.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Multi-Zone High Availability

Multi-VSwitch Architecture

Auto Scaling groups reside within a single Region, but can span multiple VSwitches across distinct Availability Zones (AZs):

  • Zone-Level Fault Domain Isolation: If a physical datacenter event affects Zone A, workloads continue uninterrupted across Zones B and C.
  • Single VPC CIDR: All VSwitches belong to the same parent VPC, enabling seamless private intranet routing between all scaled instances.
  • Subnet Quota Safeguard: Spreading across multiple VSwitches prevents IP address exhaustion within any individual CIDR block.

Cross-Zone Inventory Resilience

How multi-zone configuration protects against resource stock-outs:

  • Inventory Hedging: Cloud instance families can temporarily run out of stock in a single zone during massive regional flash events.
  • Automatic Zone Failover: By binding multiple VSwitches in different zones, Auto Scaling automatically provisions capacity in alternate zones when the primary zone is depleted.
  • SLB Multi-AZ Synergy: Fronting the multi-zone scaling group with a Multi-AZ SLB/ALB guarantees complete end-to-end disaster recovery.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Multi-Zone Allocation Policies

Allocation Policy Scale-Out Mechanism Scale-In Mechanism Recommended Enterprise Workload
Priority Policy
Strict Sequential		 Provisions 100% of instances in the first configured VSwitch (Zone A). Only fails over to Priority 2 (Zone B) if Zone A runs out of inventory or IP quota. Removes instances in reverse priority order: releases instances in Zone C first, then Zone B, and lastly Zone A. Latency-sensitive workloads that benefit from co-locating instances within a single physical datacenter to minimize intra-cluster network latency.
Balanced Distribution
Equalized Spread		 Evenly distributes instances across all configured VSwitches/Zones. If 9 instances are requested across 3 zones, exactly 3 instances are created per zone. Selects instances from the zone with the highest current instance count to rebalance and maintain equal proportion across all zones. Mission-critical production web applications, e-commerce storefronts, and microservices requiring maximum multi-zone fault isolation.
Cost-Optimized Policy
Spot & Price Focused		 Evaluates real-time hourly spot pricing and inventory availability across all zones, provisioning in the lowest-cost zone first. Removes the highest-cost instances first to optimize ongoing cloud spend. Fault-tolerant big data batch processing, rendering farms, and offline machine learning training clusters.
Architectural Recommendation For standard enterprise production, always select Balanced Distribution across at least 3 availability zones. This ensures that an unexpected outage in any single zone will never affect more than 33% of your active serving fleet.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Instance Reclaim Modes: Release vs. Shutdown

1. Release Mode (Default)

Instances are completely terminated and destroyed during scale-in:

  • Zero Ongoing Billing: All compute (vCPU, RAM), local disks, and system disks are deleted. Absolutely no ongoing compute charges are incurred.
  • Stateless Architecture: Designed strictly for stateless application tiers where application code and dependencies are baked into custom images or pulled on boot.
  • Startup Duration: When scaling out again, new instances must undergo cold OS provisioning, cloud-init scripts, and disk initialization (~2-5 minutes).
  • Best For: Highly variable, bursty web traffic and non-urgent scale-outs where cost minimization is top priority.

2. Shutdown & Reclaim Mode (Recycle)

Instances are stopped rather than destroyed during scale-in:

  • Stopped State: Instances transition to Stopped status. Compute vCPU and RAM billing stops under No-Fee Stopped mode (if qualified).
  • Retained Disks & IPs: System disks, data disks, and private IP addresses are retained (storage disk fees continue to apply).
  • Rapid Warm Start: Scaling out merely boots existing stopped instances, cutting spin-up time down to 30-60 seconds (bypassing disk provisioning and cloud-init).
  • Best For: Heavy application stacks with long initial startup times (e.g., massive Java JVM warms or large game servers) requiring rapid surge response.
Billing Note In Shutdown & Reclaim Mode, while compute vCPU and RAM billing ceases under Stopped mode, Cloud Disk storage fees continue to accrue for all stopped disks. Use Release Mode for maximum cost elimination on purely stateless workloads.
Section 2: Scaling Groups & Capacity Design

Auto-Created vs. Manually Attached Instances

Lifecycle Dimension Auto-Created Instances Manually Attached Instances
Creation Mechanism Provisioned automatically by Auto Scaling activities based on the active Scaling Configuration. Created independently by administrators via ECS Console/CLI, then manually added into the Scaling Group.
Configuration Association Strictly governed by the active Scaling Configuration / Launch Template. Independent of the Scaling Configuration; can use different instance types, images, or specs.
Billing Type Pay-As-You-Go or Spot Instances only. Can be Subscription, Pay-As-You-Go, or Preemptible (Spot) instances.
Scale-In Removal Behavior Terminated/released (Release Mode) or stopped (Shutdown Mode) according to group policy. Detached only! Manually attached instances are NEVER terminated or stopped by Auto Scaling upon scale-in.
SLB & RDS Management Automatically registered and deregistered with SLB and RDS whitelists. Automatically registered to SLB and RDS upon joining group, and deregistered upon detachment.
Removal Priority Removed based on group removal policy (e.g. OldestInstance or OldestScalingConfiguration). Removed first or last depending on configured policy, but always preserved in running state.
Safety Guarantee You can safely attach existing production ECS instances (such as primary application nodes or Subscription instances) to a scaling group. Auto Scaling will never delete or shut down manually attached instances during scale-in activities.
Section 3: Scaling Configurations & Blueprints

Scaling Configurations & Blueprints

What is a Scaling Configuration?

A Scaling Configuration acts as the golden master template for all automatically provisioned ECS instances:

  • Compute Specification: Instance family and size (e.g. ecs.g8i.xlarge) or multi-type fallbacks.
  • Operating System Image: Public image (Alibaba Cloud Linux, Ubuntu) or verified enterprise Custom Image with pre-installed software.
  • Storage Architecture: System disk type (ESSD AutoPL, PL0-PL3), disk capacity, and optional data disk mounts.
  • Security Credentials: Security Groups, SSH Key Pairs, and RAM Roles for secure metadata credential retrieval.
  • Bootstrapping User Data: Cloud-init scripts executed on boot to configure software and register agents.

Configuration Lifecycle & State Machine

Managing configurations within a Scaling Group:

  • Active vs. Inactive: A Scaling Group can store up to 10 Scaling Configurations, but exactly ONE configuration can be Active at any time.
  • Immutable Versioning: A Scaling Configuration cannot be modified once created. To change specifications, create a new configuration and set it to Active.
  • Deletion Constraints:
    • An Active Scaling Configuration cannot be deleted.
    • A configuration cannot be deleted if active instances created by it still exist in the group.
Best Practice For modern enterprise deployments, use **ECS Launch Templates** instead of legacy Scaling Configurations. Launch Templates provide native multi-version management and allow seamless parameter sharing between Auto Scaling, ACK, and manual ECS provisioning.
Section 3: Scaling Configurations & Blueprints

Launch Templates Integration

Why Use Launch Templates?

Alibaba Cloud ECS Launch Templates decouple configuration definitions from individual services:

  • Unified Template Library: Share identical instance configurations across Auto Scaling, Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK), and manual provisioning.
  • Built-in Version Control: Maintain multiple numbered versions (e.g. Version 1, Version 2) with change logs. Auto Scaling can bind to a specific version or track the dynamic Default Version.
  • Template Overrides: Specify custom parameters on top of standard template definitions without re-authoring the base template.

Zero-Downtime Blue-Green Fleet Rotation

Seamless application deployment workflow using Launch Template versions:

  1. Step 1: Build new application release and capture a new Custom Image (e.g. v2.4.0).
  2. Step 2: Create a new version of the ECS Launch Template referencing the updated Image ID.
  3. Step 3: Update the Auto Scaling group to point to the new Launch Template version.
  4. Step 4: Auto Scaling smoothly rotates the fleet: as instances scale out, they automatically boot the new version, while old instances are gracefully retired via scale-in.
Cloud-Native Standard Launch Templates eliminate the legacy 10-configuration limit per scaling group and allow centralizing security, storage, and networking governance across organizational teams.
Section 3: Scaling Configurations & Blueprints

Multi-Instance Type Configuration

The Stock-Out Problem (Single Type Risk)

Relying on a single ECS instance type in a scaling configuration creates a single point of failure:

  • During massive regional flash events (e.g., 11.11 Global Shopping Festival), popular instance sizes (like ecs.c8i.2xlarge) can temporarily run out of datacenter stock.
  • If only one type is specified, the entire scaling activity fails, leaving your application under-provisioned and vulnerable to traffic overload.

Configuring Multi-Instance Type Fallback Pools

Auto Scaling allows specifying up to 10 instance types in a prioritized list:

  • Automatic Sequential Fallback: If Type 1 is out of inventory, Auto Scaling immediately attempts Type 2, Type 3, etc., ensuring 100% scale-out success.
  • Cross-Architecture Hedging: Mix Intel, AMD, and ARM Yitian instances with equivalent vCPU-to-memory ratios:
    • Priority 1: ecs.g8i.2xlarge (Intel Sapphire Rapids, 8 vCPU / 32 GiB)
    • Priority 2: ecs.g8a.2xlarge (AMD Genoa, 8 vCPU / 32 GiB)
    • Priority 3: ecs.g8y.2xlarge (Alibaba Yitian 710 ARM, 8 vCPU / 32 GiB)
    • Priority 4: ecs.g7.2xlarge (Previous Generation Fallback)
High Availability Rule In production environments, never configure a Scaling Configuration with only one instance type. Always specify at least 3 to 5 equivalent instance families to guarantee inventory availability during regional spikes.
Section 3: Scaling Configurations & Blueprints

Preemptible (Spot) Instances & Mixed Pools

Preemptible (Spot) Instance Mechanics

Harness excess Alibaba Cloud datacenter capacity at up to 90% discount compared to Pay-As-You-Go rates:

  • Market-Driven Pricing: Price fluctuates in real time based on datacenter supply and demand.
  • Reclaim Notice: If market price exceeds your bid or capacity is needed for full-price customers, instances receive a 5-minute eviction warning.
  • Spot Strategy in Auto Scaling:
    • No Spot Protection: Follows real-time market prices without duration guarantee.
    • 1-Hour Protection Period: Guarantees non-interruption for the initial 60 minutes.

Mixed On-Demand & Spot Allocation Pools

Auto Scaling combines reliability and extreme cost reduction in a single group:

  • Base Capacity (On-Demand): Maintain a fixed baseline (e.g. 5 Pay-As-You-Go instances) to ensure core services never drop below safe limits.
  • Surge Capacity (Spot Instances): Any capacity above the baseline is fulfilled with Spot instances for peak loads.
  • Capacity-Optimized Spot Allocation: Auto Scaling analyzes price trends and historical interruption rates across multiple instance types, picking the spot types least likely to be reclaimed.
  • Auto-Replacement on Eviction: When a spot instance is evicted, Auto Scaling immediately spins up a replacement instance automatically.
Enterprise Architecture Pattern Stateless web frontends, API gateways, and asynchronous queue workers achieve 70%+ infrastructure cost savings by pairing a 20% On-Demand baseline with an 80% Spot burst pool.
Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Scaling Rule Types

Rule Type Operational Logic Evaluation Method Best Use Case
Simple Scaling Rule Executes a fixed action: Add N, Remove N, or Set Total to N. Executed directly by scheduled tasks or manual API invocation. Predictable scheduled spikes (daily start-of-day traffic, weekly marketing emails).
Step Scaling Rule Applies tiered responses based on the magnitude of the metric breach (e.g. CPU 70-80% add 2; CPU >80% add 6). CloudMonitor alarm multi-step metric breach evaluations. Rapidly accelerating surges where larger capacity boosts are required for severe overloads.
Target Tracking Rule Continuously adjusts capacity to keep a specific metric at a defined target value (e.g. Average CPU = 50%). Auto-calculates required instance adjustments like a thermostat. Standard microservice clusters with smooth, continuous traffic fluctuations.
Predictive Scaling Rule Uses machine learning algorithms to forecast demand 24-48 hours ahead based on historical CloudMonitor curves. Generates predictive scaling plans and pre-warms capacity before the surge arrives. Large enterprise applications with slow cold-boot times (5-10 mins) and repetitive weekly traffic cycles.
Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Simple Scaling & Step Scaling Rules

Simple Scaling Rules

The fundamental building block of scaling actions:

  • Adjustment Types:
    • Quantity Adjustment: Add 2 or Remove 1 instance.
    • Percentage Adjustment: Add 30% of current capacity (rounds to nearest integer).
    • Total Capacity Adjustment: Adjust to 10 instances directly.
  • Boundary Enforcement: If Total = 4 and rule says Remove 5 with MinSize = 2, Auto Scaling removes only 2 instances.
  • Cooldown Enforced: If triggered by an alarm, the scaling group enters cooldown immediately after the activity completes.

Step Scaling Rules (Proportional Response)

Dynamically scales based on the severity of load breach:

Metric Condition (CPU) Scaling Action Resulting Behavior
70% ≤ CPU < 80% Add 2 Instances Moderate growth response
80% ≤ CPU < 90% Add 5 Instances Aggressive scale-out
CPU ≥ 90% Add 10 Instances Emergency burst rescue

Zero Cooldown Blocking on Step Ups: If metric load continues rising into a higher step tier, step scaling can add additional capacity immediately without waiting for cooldown!

Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Target Tracking Scaling Rules

How Target Tracking Works

Operates like a self-regulating building thermostat:

  • Instead of defining manual thresholds ("If CPU > 80% add 2"), you define a desired steady-state target metric: e.g., Maintain Average CPU at 50%.
  • Auto Scaling automatically monitors the metric and continuously calculates the exact mathematical number of instances required: 
    Target Capacity = Current Capacity × (Current Metric Value / Target Value)
  • Automatically generates paired scale-out and scale-in alarms behind the scenes.

Supported Target Metrics & Best Practices

Pre-defined metrics optimized for target tracking:

  • CpuUtilization: Average CPU usage across the cluster (ideal target: 40% to 60%).
  • IntranetIn / IntranetOut: Average inbound or outbound network traffic per instance.
  • ClassicLoadBalancerQps: Average queries per second (QPS) distributed by SLB to each backend ECS instance.
Conservative Scale-In Target tracking scales out aggressively to preserve performance, but scales in conservatively to prevent capacity flapping during temporary metric dips.
Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Predictive Scaling Rules (AI & Machine Learning)

The VM Boot Latency Challenge

Why reactive metric alarms fall short for heavy enterprise applications:

  • Standard ECS instances take 2 to 5 minutes to boot the OS, initialize JVMs, warm caches, and join SLB backends.
  • During sudden viral surges, reactive CloudMonitor alarms trigger after CPU hits 80%. By the time new VMs are ready 5 minutes later, users have already suffered timeouts and dropped connections.

Proactive Pre-Warming via Deep Learning

Predictive scaling utilizes Alibaba Cloud machine learning algorithms to eliminate cold-start delays:

  • Historical Pattern Recognition: Analyzes minimum 24 hours (ideally several weeks) of CloudMonitor telemetry to identify repetitive daily and weekly business cycles.
  • Forecast Horizon: Generates automated scaling predictions for the next 48 hours, updating the prediction model every 24 hours.
  • Pre-Warming Buffer: Automatically provisions instances 15 to 30 minutes BEFORE the anticipated traffic spike arrives, ensuring servers are 100% warmed and healthy when traffic hits.
  • Safety Fallback: Operates alongside reactive dynamic alarms: if an unpredicted sudden surge exceeds the ML prediction, dynamic alarms instantly scale out extra capacity.
Enterprise Architecture Pattern Combine **Predictive Scaling** (to pre-warm capacity for expected peak hours) with **Target Tracking** (to absorb unexpected real-time spikes). This dual-layer strategy delivers the ultimate combination of SLA stability and cost control.
Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Event-Triggered Alarm Tasks (CloudMonitor)

CloudMonitor Integration Architecture

Event-triggered tasks bridge real-time infrastructure telemetry with Auto Scaling actions:

  • CloudMonitor agents collect system performance metrics across all ECS instances in the scaling group.
  • Aggregated statistics (Average, Maximum, Minimum) are computed across the cluster over specified evaluation windows (e.g. 1 min, 5 min).
  • When the metric breaches the configured threshold for N consecutive evaluation periods (e.g. 3 periods), CloudMonitor invokes the Auto Scaling API to execute the assigned Scaling Rule.

Key Supported Metrics

Metric Name Measurement Unit Common Threshold Trigger
CPU Utilization Percentage (%) Scale-Out: ≥ 75% | Scale-In: ≤ 25%
Memory Utilization Percentage (%) Scale-Out: ≥ 80% | Scale-In: ≤ 30%
Intranet In / Out Bytes / sec (Bps) Detects high network streaming or batch data ingestion
System Disk Read / Write IOPS / Bps Detects disk I/O bottlenecks and log queue backups
TCP Connection Count Established connections Detects massive concurrent user connection surges
Cooldown Rule During the cooldown period, CloudMonitor alarm requests are REJECTED by the Scaling Group. This deliberate lockout prevents runaway over-scaling while newly created instances are still booting.
Section 4: Scaling Rules & Trigger Mechanisms

Scheduled & Recurring Tasks

Scheduled Task Parameters

Executes a scaling rule at a predetermined date, time, or recurrence interval:

  • One-Time Execution: Triggers at an exact future timestamp (e.g., 2026-11-11 00:00:00 for a midnight product launch).
  • Recurring Schedules: Uses standard cron expressions (e.g. 0 0 8 * * ? to scale up at 08:00 every morning).
  • Launch Expiration Time: The maximum time window (in seconds, up to 21,600s / 6 hours) that a scheduled task will wait and retry if the group is currently busy executing another activity. If the window expires, the task is abandoned.

Execution Conflict & Priority Rules

How Auto Scaling resolves scheduled task conflicts:

  • Bypasses Cooldown Period: Unlike CloudMonitor alarms, Scheduled Tasks execute immediately without waiting for cooldown time to expire!
  • One Activity at a Time: If a scheduled task arrives while another scaling activity is running, it retries continuously within its Launch Expiration Time window.
  • Simultaneous Task Resolution:
    • If multiple tasks are scheduled at similar times, the earliest scheduled task triggers first. Subsequent tasks retry within their expiration windows.
    • If multiple tasks are scheduled at the exact same minute, the system executes the latest scheduled task created.
Architectural Comparison CloudMonitor Alarms are reactive and subject to cooldown locks. Scheduled Tasks are proactive and completely bypass cooldown locks.
Section 5: Lifecycle Management & Cooldown

The Cooldown Period (Anti-Flapping Mechanism)

The Purpose of Cooldown Time

The cooldown period is a mandatory stabilization window following any successful scaling activity:

  • Why It Is Critical: When new ECS instances are added, they require several minutes to complete OS booting, initialize application runtimes, and warm up caches. During this window, cluster CPU utilization remains temporarily high.
  • Preventing Flapping (Thrashing): Without a cooldown lock, CloudMonitor would continuously fire alarms every minute, adding 20 or 50 unnecessary instances before the first batch could even begin serving traffic.
  • Default Cooldown: Configurable at the Scaling Group level (default: 300 seconds / 5 minutes). Can also be overridden on individual scaling rules.

Cooldown Behavior & Task Selective Lockout

Trigger / Task Type Behavior During Cooldown Architectural Reason
CloudMonitor Alarm Tasks REJECTED Blocks reactive metrics while new instances are warming up and stabilizing load.
Scheduled Tasks EXECUTED Deterministic business schedules take precedence; scheduled tasks bypass cooldown.
Manual API Execution EXECUTED Direct human operator intent overrides automated stabilization locks.

Timer Start Point: Cooldown time begins strictly after the last ECS instance has finished being added/removed and attached to the SLB/RDS instances.

Section 5: Lifecycle Management & Cooldown

Lifecycle Hooks Architecture

Scale-Out Hook: PENDING_ADD

Suspends the instance after OS boot before joining SLB traffic:

  • Instance is created, IP allocated, and OS booted, but held in PENDING_ADD.
  • Use Cases: Download latest application code, run database migrations, execute security posture scans, and pre-load in-memory caches.
  • Action: Only after the hook completes does the instance transition to IN_SERVICE and accept incoming SLB client requests.

Scale-In Hook: PENDING_REMOVE

Suspends instance termination during scale-in:

  • Instance is removed from SLB traffic, but held alive in PENDING_REMOVE.
  • Use Cases: Complete in-flight transactions (connection draining), flush local application buffers, and upload access logs/crash dumps to OSS buckets.
  • Action: Only after the hook completes is the ECS instance actually released or stopped, guaranteeing zero data loss.
Section 5: Lifecycle Management & Cooldown

Lifecycle Hook Operations & Heartbeats

Hook State Machine Parameters

Parameter Value Range Operational Description
Default Timeout 30 to 21,600 sec (up to 6 hrs) The duration Auto Scaling suspends the instance waiting for external task completion.
Heartbeat Extension RecordLifecycleActionHeartbeat If a custom bootstrapping job requires more time, invoke this API to reset and extend the timeout clock.
Default Result (Timeout) CONTINUE or ABANDON The fallback action executed if the timeout expires before an explicit completion signal is received.

Timeout Action Decision Matrix

Choosing the correct fallback outcome when tasks exceed timeout:

  • Scale-Out (PENDING_ADD):
    • CONTINUE: Forcefully brings the instance into service and attaches it to SLB (risk: uninitialized code serves traffic).
    • ABANDON (Recommended): Aborts and releases the failed instance, then rolls back or attempts to spin up a fresh one.
  • Scale-In (PENDING_REMOVE):
    • CONTINUE (Recommended): Proceeds with instance termination/release.
    • ABANDON: Stops scale-in, detaches the instance from group, but leaves the VM running.
  • Explicit Signal: Once your script finishes, always call CompleteLifecycleAction immediately to avoid waiting for the full timeout.
Section 5: Lifecycle Management & Cooldown

Instance Removal Policies

Removal Policy Selection Criteria Architectural Impact Ideal Scenario
OldestInstance
FIFO (First-In, First-Out)		 Selects the auto-created instance with the earliest creation timestamp. Gradually rotates out older servers, preventing software state accumulation, memory leaks, and disk fragmentation. Default enterprise web clusters, long-running microservices, and general production workloads.
NewestInstance
LIFO (Last-In, First-Out)		 Selects the most recently created auto-created instance in the group. Protects established, pre-warmed servers with active connection pools and established caches. Workloads where newly spawned instances are purely temporary surge absorbers and older nodes are warm.
OldestScalingConfiguration
Fleet Modernization		 Selects instances created by the oldest, outdated Scaling Configuration first. Automatically purges legacy configuration instances from the group during natural scale-in events. Active blue-green rollouts and automated progressive fleet upgrades after releasing new image versions.
Multi-Zone Balancing Precedence In multi-zone scaling groups using Balanced Distribution, Auto Scaling first selects the availability zone with the most instances, and **then** applies the configured removal policy (e.g., OldestInstance) within that specific zone.
Section 6: Cloud-Native Integrations

Server Load Balancer (SLB/ALB) Auto-Configuration

Automated Registration Workflow

Seamless traffic distribution across dynamic instance pools:

  • Zero Manual Binding: When an ECS instance is created by Auto Scaling, it is automatically attached to the backend server groups or VServer groups of all associated SLB/ALB instances.
  • Port & Weight Assignment: Uses the backend listening ports and default forwarding weights (e.g. weight=50) configured in the scaling group.
  • Health Verification: Load balancers begin probing instance health; traffic is routed only after the instance reports passing health checks.

Graceful Scale-In & Connection Draining

How Auto Scaling terminates instances without dropping active client sessions:

  • Automatic Deregistration: When scale-in begins, Auto Scaling immediately removes the target instance from the SLB backend pool.
  • Zero New Connections: SLB stops directing any new client requests to the departing instance.
  • Connection Draining Window: Existing in-flight HTTP connections are given a configurable grace period (e.g. 60-300 seconds) to finish cleanly.
  • Safe Destruction: Only after active sessions drain and lifecycle hooks complete is the ECS instance actually destroyed.
High Availability Architecture You can associate multiple SLB instances (e.g. an external public-facing ALB for web clients and an internal private SLB for microservice RPC) with a single scaling group simultaneously.
Section 6: Cloud-Native Integrations

ApsaraDB RDS Whitelist Auto-Configuration

The Dynamic IP Security Problem

Managing database firewalls in an auto-scaled environment:

  • ApsaraDB RDS enforces strict IP whitelisting: only explicitly authorized private IP addresses can open database connections.
  • Because Auto Scaling dynamically provisions and terminates instances with changing private IPs, manual whitelist updates are impossible. Opening the database to 0.0.0.0/0 violates security compliance.

Automated Security Group Whitelisting

How Auto Scaling automates zero-trust database security:

  • Scale-Out Injection: When a new instance boots, Auto Scaling queries its private IP (e.g. 172.16.1.45) and automatically injects it into the security whitelist of all associated RDS instances.
  • Immediate Database Access: Application servers can establish connection pools and begin querying RDS tables without permission errors.
  • Scale-In Pruning: When an instance is removed or destroyed, its private IP is immediately purged from the RDS whitelist, preventing security holes or unauthorized reuse.
  • Security Group Binding (Best Practice): Alternatively, bind the ECS Security Group directly to the RDS whitelist for instant zero-configuration authorization.
Enterprise Security Compliance Automated RDS whitelisting ensures that even with dozens of dynamic scaling events per day, your database remains 100% shielded against unauthorized internal network access.
Section 6: Cloud-Native Integrations

Serverless Hybrid Scaling with ECI

Why Combine ECS and ECI?

The optimal blend of cost efficiency and instant elasticity:

  • ECS Baseline (Cost Efficiency): Run your predictable, 24/7 baseline capacity on ECS instances covered by Subscriptions or Reserved Instances for lowest unit compute pricing.
  • ECI Surge (Instant Elasticity): When sudden massive spikes exceed ECS capacity, offload surge containers directly to Elastic Container Instance (ECI) without provisioning underlying VMs.

ECI Serverless Benefits in Auto Scaling

Unmatched responsiveness during sudden traffic spikes:

  • Sub-Second Provisioning: ECI spins up container pods in seconds, completely bypassing the 2-5 minute OS boot overhead of traditional VMs.
  • Per-Second Billing: Pay strictly for the exact CPU and memory consumed during the spike duration, scaling down to zero when traffic subsides.
  • Unified SLB Routing: ALB and SLB distribute traffic across both ECS backend nodes and ECI serverless pods within the same backend group.

Section 7: Pricing Model & Cost Optimization

Enterprise Cost Optimization Strategies

1. 3-Tier Compute Sizing

The golden architecture for enterprise cloud budgeting:

  • Tier 1 (Base - 40%): Covered by 1-3 year Reserved Instances (RI) or Savings Plans (60% discount).
  • Tier 2 (Predictable - 30%): Standard Pay-As-You-Go instances scaled via scheduled rules.
  • Tier 3 (Burst - 30%): Preemptible (Spot) instances or serverless ECI for traffic peaks (90% discount).

2. Reclaim Mode Governance

Aligning reclaim behavior with workload types:

  • Stateless Web Frontends: Use Release Mode to completely destroy VMs on scale-in, eliminating 100% of idle compute and disk costs.
  • Heavy State/Cache Nodes: Use Shutdown & Reclaim Mode under No-Fee Stopped status to retain warm disks for rapid 30-second restart.

3. Metric Tuning & Damping

Preventing wasteful over-allocation:

  • Calibrate cooldown times to match real application startup times (avoiding double-scaling).
  • Use Target Tracking with conservative scale-in thresholds to avoid unnecessary compute churn.
  • Enable Predictive Scaling to pre-warm capacity without needing oversized initial baselines.
Cost Benchmark Implementing the 3-Tier Compute architecture with Auto Scaling consistently reduces total compute expenditures by **45% to 65%** compared to traditional static provisioning.
Cloud Architect Recap

Auto Scaling Resource Scoping & Boundaries

Architectural Domain Scope & Boundary Limit Architectural Mandate & Best Practice
Geographic Scope Single Region / Multi-AZ A Scaling Group cannot span multiple regions. To build cross-region disaster recovery, create independent scaling groups per region and route traffic via Global Traffic Manager (GTM).
Network Boundary Single VPC All VSwitches in a Scaling Group must belong to the same VPC. Bind multiple VSwitches across distinct AZs using Balanced Distribution.
Configuration Capacity Max 10 Configurations per Group Only 1 configuration is active at a time. Use ECS Launch Templates for unlimited versioning and cross-service standardization.
Scaling Activity Concurrency Strictly 1 Activity at a time Scaling activities are atomic and non-interruptible. Set distinct launch expiration times on overlapping scheduled tasks.
Cooldown Lockout Blocks CloudMonitor Alarms Only Default 300s. Prevents flapping while instances boot. Scheduled tasks and manual API calls bypass the cooldown period.
Instance Reclaim Safety Manual Instances are Protected Auto-created instances are terminated or stopped upon scale-in. Manually added instances are strictly detached, never destroyed.
Interactive Quiz • Scenario 1

Practice Scenario 1: Flash Sale Flapping & Cooldown Optimization

Question 1 An enterprise e-commerce platform runs a flash sale campaign where traffic spikes 5x within a 10-minute window. During the previous sale, CloudMonitor detected average CPU exceeding 80% and triggered a dynamic scale-out rule to add 5 instances. However, because the Java application required 4 minutes to boot and warm its connection pool, CPU remained above 80%. CloudMonitor continuously fired alarms every minute, ultimately creating 35 surplus instances and causing severe budget overruns and cluster thrashing. Which architectural design prevents this flapping behavior while guaranteeing fast capacity expansion?
  • A Decrease the CloudMonitor alarm threshold from 80% to 50% and reduce the evaluation period to 10 seconds.
  • B Configure the scaling group default cooldown period to 300 seconds (matching instance warm-up time), and implement a Scale-Out Lifecycle Hook (PENDING_ADD) with Target Tracking scaling to stabilize metric evaluation.
  • C Change the scaling group removal policy to NewestInstance (LIFO) and disable all SLB health checking.
  • D Convert all Pay-As-You-Go instances into Preemptible (Spot) instances with a fixed bid price.
Quiz Solution • Scenario 1

Scenario 1: Solution & Architectural Analysis

Correct Answer: B Configure Cooldown to match warm-up time & use Lifecycle Hooks with Target Tracking
Validated Architecture
✖ Option A is Incorrect
Lowering the threshold to 50% and shortening evaluation to 10 seconds severely accelerates premature alarms, worsening thrashing and triggering even more unnecessary scaling activities.
✔ Option B is Correct
Setting the cooldown period to 300s ensures CloudMonitor alarms are locked out while new instances initialize. The PENDING_ADD hook holds instances until JVM caches are warm before routing SLB traffic, eliminating flapping.
✖ Option C is Incorrect
Removal policy governs scale-in, not scale-out. Disabling SLB health checks causes traffic to be routed to booting, unready instances, producing HTTP 502/504 errors for end users.
✖ Option D is Incorrect
Spot instances alter pricing and introduce eviction risk; they do not solve metric evaluation timing, cold boot latency, or alarm over-triggering during rapid flash sales.
Interactive Quiz • Scenario 2

Practice Scenario 2: Multi-Zone High Availability & Spot Stock-Out

Question 2 A financial analytics firm deploys an Auto Scaling group to process massive daily batch computing workloads at the lowest possible cost. They configure a single Availability Zone (Zone A) with Preemptible (Spot) instances of type ecs.c8i.2xlarge. During a major cloud region compute surge, Alibaba Cloud reclaims the spot instances, and Zone A runs completely out of stock for that specific family. The scaling activities fail repeatedly, halting critical daily reports. How must the cloud architect re-design the auto scaling architecture to guarantee execution resilience?
  • A Configure the scaling group to disable ECS instance rollbacks upon scaling activity failure.
  • B Switch the scaling group to a different region and configure CEN Transit Router to tunnel traffic back.
  • C Bind multiple VSwitches across Zones A, B, and C with Balanced Distribution, and specify up to 10 equivalent instance families (Intel, AMD, ARM) in the Scaling Configuration with a mixed On-Demand/Spot allocation pool.
  • D Increase the MinSize of the scaling group to 100 instances in Zone A using exclusively Subscription billing.
Quiz Solution • Scenario 2

Scenario 2: Solution & Architectural Analysis

Correct Answer: C Multi-Zone VSwitches + Multi-Instance Types (up to 10) + Mixed On-Demand/Spot Pool
Validated Architecture
✖ Option A is Incorrect
Instance rollback is an automated platform safety feature that cleans up unattached failed instances. Disabling rollback (even if possible) does not resolve underlying physical inventory exhaustion.
✖ Option B is Incorrect
Scaling groups are strictly scoped to a single region; moving to another region adds inter-region data transfer latency, CEN transit costs, and complex routing overhead instead of solving local multi-zone design.
✔ Option C is Correct
Multi-zone VSwitches provide fault-domain failover across datacenters. Specifying up to 10 instance types across Intel, AMD, and ARM prevents stock-out bottlenecks, while an On-Demand base guarantees core capacity.
✖ Option D is Incorrect
Locking 100 instances into Subscription billing in a single zone completely defeats the elasticity goal, introduces massive fixed idle costs, and fails if Zone A experiences physical facility degradation.
Interactive Quiz • Scenario 3

Practice Scenario 3: Graceful Termination & Zero Data Loss

Question 3 A real-time multiplayer gaming backend utilizes Auto Scaling to scale in ECS instances when player traffic drops late at night. However, players frequently report that ongoing matches are abruptly severed mid-game with connection resets. Additionally, application debug and audit logs stored on local instance system disks are permanently lost when Auto Scaling destroys instances upon scale-in. How can the cloud architect guarantee zero disruption to active gameplay and 100% log preservation during automated scale-in events?
  • A Switch the instance reclaim mode from Release Mode to Shutdown and Reclaim Mode, and set MinSize equal to MaxSize.
  • B Implement a Scale-In Lifecycle Hook (PENDING_REMOVE), enable SLB connection draining, and run a script to upload local logs to OSS before sending CompleteLifecycleAction.
  • C Create a scheduled task to disable the scaling group before midnight and manually restart servers the next morning.
  • D Configure the scaling group removal policy to OldestScalingConfiguration and disable CloudMonitor alarms.
Quiz Solution • Scenario 3

Scenario 3: Solution & Architectural Analysis

Correct Answer: B Scale-In Hook (PENDING_REMOVE) + Connection Draining + Automated OSS Log Shipping
Validated Architecture
✖ Option A is Incorrect
Setting MinSize equal to MaxSize disables scaling altogether, eliminating cost efficiency. Shutdown mode preserves disks but does not solve graceful active connection termination for live gamers.
✔ Option B is Correct
The PENDING_REMOVE hook suspends VM termination. SLB connection draining allows active game matches to finish naturally without dropouts, and custom scripts upload logs to OSS before confirming completion.
✖ Option C is Incorrect
Disabling the scaling group manually defeats automation, requires nocturnal human operations, and leaves unutilized servers running at full cost all night long.
✖ Option D is Incorrect
OldestScalingConfiguration merely alters which instance is selected for removal; it provides zero connection draining grace period and cannot prevent abrupt game disconnects or disk data loss.
